title: Bangladesh | Bangladesh Bank ICT Security, Cybersecurity Framework and Data Protection
tagline: Meet Bangladesh Bank's ICT Security Guideline and 2026 Cybersecurity Framework: phishing, ICT risk, 72-hour reporting and the new data and cyber laws.
description:
This quest teaches the ICT and cyber security rules that Bangladesh Bank sets for the institutions it regulates. It is based on Bangladesh Bank's **Guideline on ICT Security, Version 4.0** (issued by BRPD Circular No. 10 of 19 June 2023) and its **Cybersecurity Framework, Version 1.0** (issued by BRPD-2 Circular No. 02 of 29 March 2026, with compliance due by 31 December 2026), and it introduces in general terms the **Cyber Security Act 2026** and the **Personal Data Protection Act 2026**.

The ICT Security Guideline requires security awareness training for all staff as early as possible after joining and every year after that, and an email security session for every new joiner within 60 days. The framework adds periodic training for all staff on security policies and cyber hygiene, and role training for privileged users, executives, security staff and vendors. This quest supports those duties for branch, operations, ICT and security staff, managers and auditors, at induction and as an annual refresher.

In five stages you join the Cyber Security Unit of a fictional Bangladeshi bank: mapping the rules, beating phishing, governing ICT risk, handling a ransomware incident against the 72-hour clock and preparing for the 31 December 2026 deadline.

The quest builds knowledge and does not replace your institution's own ICT Security Policy, procedures and training; always follow them and the latest Bangladesh Bank instructions.
audience: All staff of banks and other Bangladesh Bank-regulated institutions who need annual security awareness and the email security session
Branch managers, operations and customer service staff who handle customer data, payments and suspicious messages
ICT, information security, SOC and CIRT staff, system administrators and developers with privileged access
Managers, CISOs, risk and compliance officers who run ICT governance, ICT risk and incident reporting
Internal and IS auditors and training teams preparing for Bangladesh Bank ICT inspections
outcomes: Explain how the ICT Security Guideline v4.0, the Cybersecurity Framework v1.0, the Cyber Security Act 2026 and the PDPA 2026 fit together
Spot and report phishing, vishing, smishing and pretexting, and follow the guideline's email, device and work-from-home rules
Describe ICT governance roles and run the ICT risk cycle with sound access and privileged-user controls
Handle a cyber incident with the right roles and report critical incidents within 72 hours of occurrence
Apply the PDPA 2026 basics on consent, disclosure, security and breach notice to customer data
Build training records and evidence that meet the joining, 60-day and annual training duties

sessions.title: The Rulebook: ICT Security Guideline v4.0, the 2026 Cybersecurity Framework and the New Laws
sessions.summary: Map the rules a Bangladeshi bank works under for ICT and cyber security: Bangladesh Bank's ICT Security Guideline v4.0 (2023), its Cybersecurity Framework v1.0 (2026) with compliance due by 31 December 2026, the Cyber Security Act 2026 and the Personal Data Protection Act 2026, and the training duties they set for every member of staff.
objectives: Explain how the ICT Security Guideline v4.0, the Cybersecurity Framework v1.0 and the bank's own policy fit together
Name the institutions each Bangladesh Bank document applies to and the 31 December 2026 compliance date
Describe the awareness and training duties: on joining, every year, and the email session within 60 days
Use the 2016 cyber fraud on Bangladesh Bank's own account to explain why these rules exist

cards.title: Day one at Shimul Commercial Bank
cards.setting: Cyber Security Unit, Shimul Commercial Bank PLC head office, Motijheel, Dhaka. 9:10 am, early November 2026.

lines.text: You have just joined the Cyber Security Unit of Shimul Commercial Bank PLC. Bangladesh Bank's new Cybersecurity Framework must be met by 31 December 2026, and the board wants proof.
Welcome! I'm Farhana Akter, the CISO. Your mission: make sure every one of our 4,000 staff knows and follows the rules before the deadline. Five stages, then the inspector's exam.
Rashedul Islam, Head of ICT Division. My teams run the core banking system, SWIFT and the data centre. We already follow the ICT Security Guideline. Is the framework something new on top?
Proshanta Kumar Das, Head of the Training Institute. I need to know exactly what the rules say about training: who, when and how often.
(on video from Khulna) Sumaiya Haque, Branch Manager, KDA Avenue. Two of my officers got an email this morning that looked like it came from head office. One clicked the link.
That is exactly why we start with the rulebook. Let's open the vault.

scenes.heading: ICT Security Guideline v4.0
scenes.narration: Bangladesh Bank issued version 4.0 of its Guideline on ICT Security in June 2023 through BRPD Circular No. 10. It sets minimum controls for governance, risk, infrastructure, cyber security, access, continuity, payments, vendors and training.

scenes.heading: Cybersecurity Framework v1.0
scenes.narration: In March 2026, BRPD-2 Circular No. 02 issued the Cybersecurity Framework, Version 1.0. It is built around NIST-style functions, from preparation and governance to reporting, and must be complied with by 31 December 2026.

scenes.heading: Cyber Security Act 2026
scenes.narration: Parliament passed the Cyber Security Act in April 2026. It sets up the National Cyber Security Agency, lets the Government declare critical information infrastructure and defines cyber offences.

scenes.heading: Personal Data Protection Act 2026
scenes.narration: The Personal Data Protection Act 2026 treats personal data as belonging to the person. It sets rules on consent, disclosure, security, retention and breach notification.

scenes.heading: Your bank's own policy
scenes.narration: Each bank turns all of this into a board-approved ICT Security Policy and procedures. That policy is what you follow day to day, so it must match the guideline and the framework.

The Guideline on ICT Security, Version 4.0 (2023)

cards.title: Who the rules apply to
cards.body:
Both Bangladesh Bank documents reach well beyond scheduled banks.

- **ICT Security Guideline v4.0 (section 1.2):** banks, non-bank financial institutions, mobile financial service providers, payment service providers, payment system operators, white label ATM and merchant acquirers, and other financial service providers Bangladesh Bank regulates. The guideline calls them all "the Organization".
- **Cybersecurity Framework v1.0 (section 1.1):** banks, financial institutions, MFS providers, PSPs, PSOs and other financial or payment service providers.

The guideline describes itself as a **minimum** requirement. The framework is a **baseline** of controls, mostly drawn from ISO 27001, Bangladesh's national ICT security policies and the ICT Security Guideline itself.

If a bank cannot comply, section 1.3 of the guideline expects a named team to monitor compliance, a time-bound fix, and, if that fails, a request to Bangladesh Bank for **dispensation**. Repeated failure can lead to a penalty, depending on the impact on the business and on customers.

cards.title: Real case: the 2016 cyber fraud on Bangladesh Bank
cards.body:
Bangladesh Bank's own audited accounts for 2015-2016 record that in **February 2016** the Federal Reserve Bank of New York processed several **unauthorised transactions** from Bangladesh Bank's account there. About **USD 81 million** was paid into third-party accounts at Rizal Commercial Banking Corporation (RCBC) in the Philippines.

Bangladesh Bank told RCBC to halt onward payments, but much of the money had already been paid out to other recipients. The Philippines' Anti-Money Laundering Council secretariat recovered part of it, and the Philippine central bank fined RCBC.

In 2019, Bangladesh Bank and the New York Fed signed a Resolution and Assistance Agreement under which the New York Fed gives technical help in Bangladesh Bank's litigation to recover the funds. Their joint statement called this kind of fraud a threat to the international funds transfer system.

**Lesson:** one compromised payment channel at a central bank cost tens of millions of dollars. Today's ICT guideline has a dedicated SWIFT section and both documents put heavy weight on staff awareness.

cards.title: The clicked link
cards.setting: Video call between head office and the KDA Avenue branch, Khulna. 11:30 am.

lines.text: The email said 'Revised leave policy from HR', with a link. Officer Tanvir clicked it and typed his network password. Then he realised the sender's address was slightly wrong.
Good that he noticed. Has he reported it formally, or just told you?
Just told me. He joined us six weeks ago. Has he even had the email security session yet?
Let me check... his induction was in Dhaka, but the email security session for his batch is scheduled for next month.
Anisur Rahman Talukder, Head of ICT Audit. Next month would be past 60 days. An inspector would flag that.
Then we have two jobs: handle this incident, and fix the training calendar.

cards.title: What first?
cards.situation: Officer Tanvir at the Khulna branch entered his network password on a page reached from a suspicious email. He has told his manager but not the IT help desk or the Cyber Security Unit. It is 11:35 am and he is still logged in to the core banking system.

choices.text: Report it at once through the bank's incident channel, have his password reset after his identity is verified, and let the Cyber Security Unit check his account activity.
choices.outcome: Right. The guideline expects abnormal activity to be reported immediately and identity to be verified before credentials are changed. The unit can now look for misuse of his account and block the phishing site.

choices.text: Tell Tanvir to change his own password now and say nothing more, to avoid embarrassing him.
choices.outcome: Partly helpful, but the attacker may already have used the password, and nobody is checking. Silence also stops the unit from warning others who got the same email.

choices.text: Wait for the email security session next month, where Tanvir can raise it.
choices.outcome: Poor. The stolen password can be used today. Incidents must go through the reporting channel straight away, not wait for training.

choices.text: Forward the phishing email to all branch staff with the warning 'do not click this'.
choices.outcome: Risky. Sending a live malicious link around the branch spreads it further. The Cyber Security Unit decides how to warn staff safely.

cards.question: Which statement about the yearly email security refresher in section 5.14.9 of the ICT Security Guideline is accurate?
options: It is mandatory for every employee, with no exceptions
It is recommended for all staff; the session within 60 days of joining is the firm requirement
It is only for email administrators and IT staff
It replaces the annual security awareness training in section 6.7.1
cards.explanation: Section 5.14.9 requires the session within 60 days of joining and recommends a yearly refresher. Separately, section 6.7.1 requires security awareness training for all staff on joining and every year after, so the yearly cycle still happens.

cards.title: How to keep the rulebook straight
cards.body:
- Quote the **document and section** when you explain a rule: 'ICT Guideline 6.7.1' or 'Framework 8.1.2.1'.
- Use the **bank's ICT Security Policy** for day-to-day steps; it must comply with the guideline.
- When a Bangladesh Bank circular and a training plan disagree, the circular wins; flag the gap to the CISO.
- Laws change: the Cyber Security Act 2026 was already amended in July 2026. Check the current text on the Laws of Bangladesh portal before quoting it.

cards.title: Stage 1 take-aways
items: The ICT Security Guideline v4.0 (BRPD Circular 10, June 2023) sets minimum ICT controls for all Bangladesh Bank-regulated financial service providers.
The Cybersecurity Framework v1.0 (BRPD-2 Circular 02, March 2026) adds a seven-function baseline; compliance is due by 31 December 2026.
All staff need security awareness on joining and every year; new joiners need an email security session within 60 days.
The Cyber Security Act 2026 and the Personal Data Protection Act 2026 now sit above the Bangladesh Bank rules.
The 2016 cyber fraud on Bangladesh Bank's New York Fed account shows what a payment channel compromise can cost.

cards.prompt: Think about your own first weeks in your bank. When did you receive security awareness and an email security session? If it was later than the rules expect, what would you change for the next batch of joiners?

quiz.question: Which Bangladesh Bank circular issued the Guideline on ICT Security, Version 4.0?
options: BRPD-2 Circular No. 02 of 29 March 2026
BRPD-1 Circular No. 10 of 7 May 2026
BRPD Circular No. 10 of 19 June 2023
BFIU Circular No. 26 of 16 June 2020
quiz.explanation: Version 4.0 of the ICT Security Guideline was issued by BRPD Circular No. 10 of 19 June 2023. BRPD-2 Circular No. 02 of 2026 issued the Cybersecurity Framework instead.

quiz.question: By what date must institutions covered by Bangladesh Bank's Cybersecurity Framework v1.0 comply with it?
options: 30 June 2026, the end of the fiscal year
29 March 2027, one year after issue
No date; it is voluntary guidance
31 December 2026
quiz.explanation: BRPD-2 Circular No. 02 of 29 March 2026 requires compliance with the framework by 31 December 2026.

quiz.question: A payment service provider licensed by Bangladesh Bank says the ICT Security Guideline is only for scheduled banks. Is that right?
options: No. Section 1.2 applies it to banks, NBFIs, MFS providers, PSPs, PSOs and other Bangladesh Bank-regulated providers.
Yes. Only scheduled banks are named in the guideline's applicability section.
Yes, unless the PSP also holds a full banking licence.
No, but PSPs need only follow the chapter on digital payment security.
quiz.explanation: Section 1.2 lists banks, NBFIs, MFS providers, PSPs, PSOs, white label ATM and merchant acquirers and other regulated providers, calling them all 'the Organization'.

quiz.question: Under section 6.7.1 of the ICT Security Guideline, when must security awareness training be given to staff?
options: Only when a member of staff is promoted to an officer grade
As early as possible after joining, and every year after that
Every three years, or sooner after a serious security incident at the bank
Once at induction, with no repeat required
quiz.explanation: Section 6.7.1 requires security awareness training for all staff at the earliest possible time after they start and annually thereafter, including spotting social engineering and resisting phishing.

quiz.question: Rafiq joined a bank on 1 August. Under section 5.14.9 of the ICT Security Guideline, by when should he have attended the email security awareness session?
options: Within 30 days of joining, so by the end of August
By the end of the calendar year
Within 60 days of joining, so by about the end of September
Within 90 days of joining, so at his probation confirmation review
quiz.explanation: The guideline requires an email security awareness session for all new joiners within 60 days of their enrolment, covering phishing detection, email etiquette and internal incident reporting.

quiz.question: What does section 1.3 of the ICT Security Guideline expect when a bank cannot fix a non-compliance within its time frame?
options: Seek dispensation from Bangladesh Bank; repeated failure may lead to a penalty
Report the matter to the National Cyber Security Agency, which can extend the deadline
Nothing; the guideline is advisory, so there are no consequences
Suspend the services affected until the next external audit
quiz.explanation: Section 1.3 asks for a monitoring team, a time-bound fix and, if that fails, a request for dispensation. After repeated failures a penalty may follow, depending on the impact on business or customers.

quiz.question: Which list gives the seven functions named in Bangladesh Bank's Cybersecurity Framework v1.0?
options: Plan, Do, Check, Act, Audit, Report and Improve
Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover, exactly as in the original NIST model
Govern, Assess, Contain, Eradicate, Recover, Notify and Close
Preparation and Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recovery and Reporting
quiz.explanation: The framework aligns with NIST but adds its own structure: seven functions from Preparation and Govern through to Reporting.

quiz.question: A new officer clicked a link in a fake HR email and typed her password. Her branch manager suggests waiting for the next training session to discuss it. What should happen instead?
options: Wait, because the email session within 60 days will cover it anyway
Report it now through the incident channel, so her account can be checked and the password reset after verifying her identity
Ask her to forward the email to colleagues so they can recognise it
Reset the password quietly and close the matter without a record
quiz.explanation: Abnormal activity must be reported immediately, and identity must be verified before credentials are changed. Forwarding a live link spreads it; silence leaves misuse undetected.

quiz.question: According to Bangladesh Bank's 2015-2016 accounts, what happened to its account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York in February 2016?
options: A systems outage stopped all of its foreign currency payments through the New York Fed for a week
Its customer records were stolen and offered for sale
Unauthorised transactions paid about USD 81 million to accounts at RCBC in the Philippines
A ransomware attack encrypted its reserve management system
quiz.explanation: The accounts record unauthorised transactions processed by the New York Fed that paid about USD 81 million into third-party accounts at RCBC in the Philippines, much of which was then paid onward.

quiz.question: The framework says one of its controls conflicts with an Act of the Government of Bangladesh. Which applies?
options: The Act prevails over the framework control
The framework control prevails because it is more specific
The bank may choose whichever is stricter for it
Neither applies until Bangladesh Bank issues a new circular
quiz.explanation: The framework's disclaimer says Government Acts, laws, guidelines and policies supersede a conflicting control. A conflict with another Bangladesh Bank instruction can be resolved on request.

sessions.title: Phishing, Email Security and Social Engineering at the Desk
sessions.summary: Apply the ICT Security Guideline's email, social engineering, end-user device, work-from-home and social media banking rules: spot phishing and pretexting, handle confidential information by email, verify identity before credential changes and report suspicious activity at once.
objectives: Recognise phishing, vishing, smishing and pretexting attempts aimed at bank staff and customers
Apply the guideline's email rules on attachments, links, encryption, classification and corporate addresses
Verify identity before any password reset or token change, and refuse to reveal internal information
Follow desk, device and work-from-home rules and report abnormal activity immediately

cards.title: The fake leave policy
cards.setting: Cyber Security Unit, Motijheel. 2:00 pm, the same day.

lines.text: The 'HR leave policy' email reached 214 staff. Eleven clicked. Three typed their passwords. We've reset all three and blocked the domain.
The sender's domain swapped one letter in our name. The display name said 'HR Division'. Our mail filter let it through because the domain was brand new.
My officers say they were busy at the counter. They didn't have time to check every sender.
Then the training has to give them a habit that takes five seconds, not five minutes.
Exactly. This stage is the Inbox Ghat: every message that lands on our shore gets checked before anyone steps on board.

cards.title: How a phishing attack on a bank unfolds

scenes.heading: The lure
scenes.narration: The attacker sends a message that looks routine: an HR notice, a Bangladesh Bank circular, a courier slip or a customer complaint. It is built to be opened without thinking.

scenes.heading: The pressure
scenes.narration: It pushes for speed: act today, your account will be locked, the MD needs this now. Urgency stops people checking the sender or the link.

scenes.heading: The hook
scenes.narration: A link leads to a fake login page, or an attachment installs malware. Short links and odd character strings hide where they really go.

scenes.heading: The catch
scenes.narration: The attacker now holds a password, a session or a foothold on a PC, and can move towards payment systems or customer data.

scenes.heading: Your counter-move
scenes.narration: Pause, check the sender and the link, never enter credentials from an email, and report it at once through the bank's channel.

cards.title: The five-second email check
cards.caption: Section 5.14.8 asks staff to avoid suspicious attachments and links and to cross-check the sender and subject before trusting a message.

items.label: Sender
items.detail: Is the address exactly right, not just the display name?

items.label: Expected?
items.detail: Were you expecting this message or attachment?

items.label: Link
items.detail: Hover first; avoid short or encoded links (guideline s.6.7.1).

items.label: Request
items.detail: Does it ask for passwords, OTPs or sensitive data?

items.label: Report
items.detail: If in doubt, report it; do not forward it around.

cards.question: Which of these is one of the end-user rules in section 6.7.1 of the ICT Security Guideline?
options: Open attachments only after business hours
Avoid clicking short code web links and encrypted character web links
Forward suspicious emails to colleagues for a second opinion
cards.explanation: Section 6.7.1 tells staff to avoid short code and encrypted character links, be suspicious of unexpected messages, never open unexpected attachments and never share sensitive information by email.

cards.title: The guideline's email rules
cards.body:
Section 5.14 of the ICT Security Guideline sets the rules every staff member must know:

- Use email only in line with the bank's policy; access comes only through an **official request**.
- **Never send confidential information to outsiders** unless it is encrypted with an approved facility; for sensitive data, use end-to-end encryption.
- **Check the data classification** before you forward or reply to anyone outside the bank.
- No defamatory, abusive or harmful content; wilful sending can lead to discipline.
- Corporate email is for business. Personal use needs management permission, and the **corporate address must not be used** for social networks, blogs or forums unless approved.
- **Avoid suspicious attachments and links**; cross-check the sender and subject.
- Outgoing mail carries a **confidentiality disclaimer**.

And section 5.14.9: every new joiner attends an **email security session within 60 days**, covering phishing detection, etiquette and how to report incidents inside the bank.

cards.title: Red flag or routine?
cards.prompt: Sort each message that reaches a branch officer.

items.text: 'Bangladesh Bank' email asking you to log in to a link to confirm your branch's SWIFT credentials
Text from an unknown number with an OTP request 'to stop your salary account being frozen'
Call from 'head office IT' asking you to read out your token code to fix a problem
Zip attachment named 'Invoice_Urgent' from a supplier you have never dealt with
Facebook page with the bank's logo offering loans if you message a WhatsApp number
Circular from your bank's intranet portal that you opened yourself
Calendar invite from your line manager's correct address for the weekly meeting
Payslip notice in the HR system you log in to directly, not via an email link

cards.back: Mass or targeted email that tricks people into clicking, opening a file or giving credentials.
Phishing tailored to one person or team, often using names, roles and real events from inside the bank.
A phone call pretending to be IT, a regulator, a senior manager or a customer, to extract codes or information.
A text or chat message with a link or a request for an OTP, PIN or account detail.
A made-up story that gives the attacker a reason to ask: an audit, a system upgrade, an urgent transfer.
A real or look-alike executive or supplier mailbox used to request payments or change bank details.

cards.title: The urgent password reset
cards.setting: ICT help desk, Shimul Commercial Bank data centre, Mirpur. 4:40 pm.

lines.text: A caller says he is the Rajshahi branch manager, locked out before an important remittance. He wants his password reset and the new one read out on the phone.
Did he give his employee ID?
He did, and he knew the branch's sub-branch names. Our help desk officer is under pressure; the caller is getting angry.
Names and IDs are easy to find. What does our procedure say about verifying identity before changing credentials?

cards.title: The angry caller
cards.situation: A caller claiming to be a branch manager demands an immediate password reset by phone. He gives a correct employee ID and is impatient. The help desk procedure requires a call-back to the number in the staff directory and approval through the ticketing system.

choices.text: Follow the procedure: end the call politely, ring back on the directory number, and reset only through the approved ticket.
choices.outcome: Best. Section 6.7.3 of the guideline requires identity to be verified before any credential is changed. The call-back reveals that the real manager never called.

choices.text: Reset the password but send it to the manager's email address rather than reading it out.
choices.outcome: Better than reading it out, but the identity has still not been verified, and if his mailbox is compromised the attacker gets the password anyway.

choices.text: Reset it because he gave the right employee ID and sub-branch names.
choices.outcome: Poor. These details are easy to collect from social media and old letters. Verification must use something the attacker cannot know or control.

choices.text: Put the caller through to the ICT Security Committee to decide.
choices.outcome: Unhelpful. The committee sets policy; it does not handle individual resets. The help desk has a procedure and must use it.

cards.title: Information you may share
cards.caption: Section 6.7.4: do not reveal personal or organisational information, including structure or networks, unless you are confident of the person's authority.

items.label: Share freely
items.detail: Public product leaflets and published branch hours.

items.label: Share after checks
items.detail: Customer data to the customer, after identity checks.

items.label: Share with authority only
items.detail: Internal structure or system names, only to verified staff with a need to know.

items.label: Never share
items.detail: Passwords, OTPs, token codes or PINs, to anyone, ever.

cards.title: A suspicious email has landed
cards.prompt: Put the right response in order.
steps: Do not click links, open attachments or reply
Check the sender address and the request against what you expect
Report it through the bank's phishing or incident channel
If you clicked or entered details, say so at once so access can be secured
Delete it only after the Cyber Security Unit confirms
Watch for the unit's follow-up alert and share lessons with your team

cards.title: At the desk: the clean desk rules
cards.body:
Section 5.12 of the guideline turns cyber hygiene into desk habits:

- **Lock your screen** before you leave your PC; the system will lock it automatically after a set time anyway.
- **USB ports are controlled**; do not plug in personal drives or phones.
- **No software installs** or downloads without authorisation.
- Laptops with sensitive data are **encrypted**, and removable media go in a **locked cabinet** when not in use.
- **Report any abnormal activity or virus at once.**

Working from home (section 5.15) adds: connect only through the bank's **VPN**, keep anti-malware updated, make sure no one can see your screen or overhear calls, and **never share a token card, smart card or credential** with anyone, including family.

On social media banking (section 11.9), the bank must watch for phishing links and fake accounts that copy its brand, block malicious URLs and take down fake posts and profiles quickly. If you see a fake page, report it; do not engage with it.

cards.question: Sumaiya's officer wants to email a customer's loan file to the customer's chartered accountant. What does section 5.14 of the guideline require first?
options: Nothing, as long as the customer asked for it
Check its classification and send it only with an approved encryption facility
Send it from a personal email so it does not burden the bank's server
Print it and post it, because email is never allowed for customer data
cards.explanation: Confidential information must not go to external parties by email unless encrypted with approved facilities, and staff must consider classification before forwarding. The customer's consent is also needed under the data protection rules.

cards.title: Habits that beat social engineering
cards.body:
- **Slow down when you feel rushed.** Urgency is the attacker's main tool.
- **Use a second channel.** Ring back on a number you already hold, not the one in the message.
- **No codes, ever.** Bank staff never need your password, OTP or token code.
- **Report, don't forward.** One report helps the unit block the attack for everyone.
- **Say it when you slip.** A quick report after a click limits the damage; hiding it multiplies it.

cards.title: Stage 2 take-aways
items: Section 6.7.1: all staff learn to spot social engineering and resist phishing on joining and every year.
Section 5.14: no confidential email to outsiders without approved encryption; check classification; avoid suspicious links and attachments.
Section 6.7.3: verify identity before any password reset, token or key change.
Never share passwords, OTPs or token codes, and do not reveal internal structure to unverified people.
Lock screens, respect USB and software controls, use the VPN at home and report abnormal activity at once.

cards.prompt: Recall the last message at work that made you feel rushed. What would the five-second check have shown? Write one habit you will start this week.

quiz.question: Which of these does section 6.7.1 of the ICT Security Guideline tell end users to do?
options: Open attachments only if antivirus is up to date
Open attachments that come from inside the country
Open attachments but disable macros first
Never open unexpected email attachments
quiz.explanation: Section 6.7.1 lists defences against phishing: be suspicious of unexpected messages, never open unexpected attachments, never share sensitive information by email and avoid clicking links in messages.

quiz.question: Under section 5.14 of the guideline, when may an officer send confidential information to an external party by email?
options: Whenever the external party is an existing, known customer of the bank
Only when it is encrypted with an approved encryption facility
Only from a personal account to protect the bank's domain
Whenever a branch manager approves it verbally
quiz.explanation: Section 5.14.3 bars sending confidential information to external parties by email unless encrypted using approved facilities. Section 5.14.12 asks for end-to-end encryption for sensitive data.

quiz.question: An officer wants to use his corporate email address to join a professional Facebook group. What does the guideline say?
options: Not unless management approves; the corporate address is not for social networks or forums
Allowed, because the group is professional
Allowed if he adds the email disclaimer to his posts
Never allowed, even with management approval
quiz.explanation: Section 5.14.7 says the corporate email address must not be used for social networking, blogs, groups or forums unless management approves.

quiz.question: A caller with a correct employee ID demands an immediate password reset. What must the help desk do under section 6.7.3?
options: Reset it because the ID matches the HR record
Reset it and send the new password by SMS to the number he gives
Verify the user's identity before changing any credential
Refuse all resets requested by phone
quiz.explanation: Section 6.7.3 requires identity verification before modifying credentials, such as password resets, new tokens or new keys. An ID number alone is easy to obtain.

quiz.question: What must the email security session for new joiners cover under section 5.14.9?
options: Configuring mail servers, spam filters and encryption keys
The penalties set by the Cyber Security Act 2026 for each kind of cyber offence by staff
Only the bank's email disclaimer and signature format
Detecting phishing emails, email etiquette and reporting incidents inside the bank
quiz.explanation: The session must cover the importance of detecting phishing, email etiquette and reporting incidents to the appropriate authority within the organisation.

quiz.question: A teller receives a text: 'Your salary account will be frozen. Share the OTP we just sent to stop it.' What kind of attack is this, and what should she do?
options: Vishing; call the number back to check
Smishing; do not reply or share the code, and report it
Spear phishing; forward it to colleagues as a warning
A routine bank alert; share the code to protect the account
quiz.explanation: A text asking for an OTP is smishing. No legitimate process needs an OTP to be shared. Reporting lets the bank warn others and block the sender.

quiz.question: Working from home, an officer's spouse asks to borrow his token card to check the family's joint account. What does section 5.15 of the guideline say?
options: Employees must not share token cards, smart cards or credentials with anyone
Sharing is acceptable within the employee's own household if the VPN stays on
Sharing is acceptable if the VPN is switched off first
Sharing is acceptable for read-only access to accounts
quiz.explanation: Section 5.15.7 bars sharing dynamic password token cards, smart cards, other access devices or credentials with anyone.

quiz.question: A visitor claiming to be from a vendor asks a branch officer which core banking version and network provider the branch uses. What does section 6.7.4 expect?
options: Share it, because vendors need it to provide support
Share it in writing, so that there is a clear record of exactly who asked for what
Give no such information unless confident of the person's authority to have it
Share it only if the visitor shows a business card
quiz.explanation: Section 6.7.4 says staff must not provide personal or organisational information, including structure or networks, unless confident of the person's authority.

quiz.question: Which practice does section 5.12 of the guideline require for desktops and laptops?
options: Leave PCs on overnight so patches can install
Lock the workstation before leaving it unattended
Allow staff to install free utilities they need
Keep USB ports open so staff can share files quickly
quiz.explanation: Section 5.12 requires locking unattended workstations, controlling USB ports, no software installation without authorisation and switching off computers at the end of the workday.

quiz.question: The bank finds a Facebook page using its logo to offer 'instant loans' through a WhatsApp number. Under section 11.9, what should the bank do?
options: Ignore it, because social media is outside the guideline
Reply publicly on the fake page to warn the fraudsters and customers away from it
Ask customers to report it to the page owner
Take down the fake page and block malicious links, and keep monitoring
quiz.explanation: Section 11.9 requires continuous monitoring for phishing links and fraudulent accounts, blocking malicious URLs and taking down malicious posts and profiles immediately.

sessions.title: ICT Governance, Cyber Roles and ICT Risk Management
sessions.summary: Learn who governs ICT and cyber risk in a Bangladeshi bank: the board, the ICT Steering and ICT Security Committees, the CISO and the risk committee; how ICT risk is identified, assessed, treated and reported; and the access, privileged-user, staff screening and vendor controls that keep risk within appetite.
objectives: Describe the roles of the board, ICT Steering Committee, ICT Security Committee, CISO and ICT Risk Management Committee
Run the guideline's ICT risk cycle, including appetite, tolerance, KRIs and the annual risk assessment
Apply access, password, privileged-user and staff screening controls from the guideline and the framework
Explain the role-based training the framework requires for administrators, developers and executives

cards.title: The board paper
cards.setting: Board meeting room, Shimul Commercial Bank PLC, Motijheel. 10:00 am, a week later.

lines.text: The board risk committee wants a one-page answer: who owns cyber risk here, and is it within our appetite?
ICT owns the systems. Doesn't that make me the owner of the risk?
Not alone. Our last IS audit found that nobody had reviewed privileged accounts on the card system for nine months. That is a governance gap, not just a technical one.
Welcome to the Control Tower. Today we sort out who decides, who does and who checks.

scenes.heading: The board
scenes.narration: The board approves the ICT strategy and the ICT Security Policy, makes sure ICT spending balances risk and benefit, ensures accountability and checks the bank's compliance with its policy.

scenes.heading: ICT Steering Committee
scenes.narration: Drawn from ICT, risk, HR, the cyber security unit, internal control and audit, legal and business units, it tracks strategic goals, guides risk and funding, prioritises projects and watches regulatory compliance.

scenes.heading: ICT Security Committee
scenes.narration: With members from ICT, cyber security, risk, internal control and business, it drives security policies, sets ICT risk thresholds and appetite with risk management, and approves changes to security processes.

scenes.heading: The CISO
scenes.narration: The framework requires a qualified CISO with the people, budget and recognised certification to lead cyber security. In the framework's incident team, the CISO is the single point of contact for users.

scenes.heading: ICT Risk Management Committee
scenes.narration: Governs overall ICT risk, reviews and approves treatment plans and receives regular reports from the security unit on the bank's ICT risk status.

cards.title: Four levels of decision (framework 2.4)
cards.caption: Information flows both ways: priorities and risk tolerance go down; progress and impact assessments come back up.

items.label: Board of Directors
items.detail: Sets mission priorities and direction for managing risk.

items.label: Senior management
items.detail: Approves the implementation strategy and takes risk decisions.

items.label: Business and process level
items.detail: Nominates the strategy, builds profiles and allocates budget.

items.label: Implementation and operations
items.detail: Puts the profiles into practice and reports progress upward.

cards.title: Match the role to the duty
cards.prompt: Link each body or person to a duty the guideline or framework gives it.

pairs.right: Approves the ICT strategy and the ICT Security Policy.
Prioritises ICT projects and guides risk, funding and sourcing.
Helps set ICT risk thresholds and appetite and approves changes to security processes.
Reviews and approves ICT risk treatment plans.
Leads cyber security and is the single point of contact for users in a cyber incident.
Carries out the internal IS audit at least once a year, using a risk-based approach.

cards.question: Who must approve the bank's ICT Security Policy under section 2.2.1 of the ICT Security Guideline?
options: The CISO
The board of directors
The ICT Steering Committee
Bangladesh Bank
cards.explanation: The bank must have an ICT Security Policy that complies with the guideline and is approved by the board, and it must be reviewed periodically.

cards.title: The ICT risk cycle
cards.body:
Chapter 3 of the guideline treats ICT risk as a **business risk**, not just an IT problem. The bank must build a documented framework with five parts:

1. **Identify** assets (each with an owner, custodian and user), threats and vulnerabilities.
2. **Assess** likely impact and likelihood, using a risk assessment matrix built on the bank's tolerance matrix.
3. **Treat** risks with controls; the ICT Risk Management Committee approves treatment plans, and residual risk is recorded.
4. **Monitor and review** new assets, threats, vulnerabilities, incidents and changes.
5. **Report** through defined lines, with a formal escalation process that says who may accept a risk.

The board or risk committee approves the **risk appetite** (how much risk the bank will accept) and **tolerance** (how far it may stray from that). **Key risk indicators** give early warning. An **ICT risk assessment must be done at least once a year**, and significant ICT risk events go into a central repository.

items.label: Identify
items.detail: Assets, owners, threats and vulnerabilities.

items.label: Assess
items.detail: Impact and likelihood against the tolerance matrix.

items.label: Treat
items.detail: Controls and approved treatment plans; record residual risk.

items.label: Monitor
items.detail: New assets, threats, incidents and changes.

items.label: Report
items.detail: Defined lines and escalation to whoever may accept risk.

cards.title: Whose control is it?
cards.prompt: Sort each control by where it sits in the bank.

items.text: Board approval of the ICT Security Policy
Risk appetite and tolerance approved by the board or risk committee
Least-privilege access granted by role and approved by the asset owner
Access revoked immediately on transfer or termination
Multi-factor authentication for critical systems
Internal IS audit at least once a year
External IS audit by a qualified auditor at least annually
Cybersecurity audit at least yearly and after any breach

cards.title: The privileged account
cards.setting: ICT Audit room, head office. 3:15 pm.

lines.text: On the card management system we found one shared 'admin' account used by four engineers and a vendor engineer, with a password unchanged for over a year.
The vendor needs it for emergency support. Splitting it would slow them down.
Speed is not a control. What does section 8.3 say about vendors and shared privileged accounts?

cards.title: Fixing the shared admin account
cards.situation: An audit finds a shared privileged account on the card management system, used by four ICT engineers and a vendor's engineer, with no individual logging. ICT says the vendor needs fast access for emergencies.

choices.text: Give each engineer a named privileged account through a privileged access tool, allow vendor access only when approved and closely supervised, and review activity logs regularly.
choices.outcome: Best. Section 8.3.2 requires restricting and reviewing privileged users, bans sharing privileged accounts and allows vendors privileged access only under close supervision and monitoring.

choices.text: Keep the shared account but change the password every 90 days.
choices.outcome: Partly better, but sharing still breaks accountability: nobody can tell who did what, and the vendor still has unsupervised access.

choices.text: Keep things as they are, because the vendor contract covers security.
choices.outcome: Poor. A contract does not move the risk. The bank remains responsible for controlling privileged access to its own systems.

choices.text: Delete the account and give all five people full administrator rights on their own logins.
choices.outcome: Poor. Named accounts help, but giving everyone full rights breaks least privilege. Access should be limited to what each role needs.

cards.title: Access numbers to remember
cards.caption: All references are to the ICT Security Guideline v4.0. The bank's own policy may set stricter values.

items.label: Password characters
items.detail: Minimum length where MFA is not used, mixing at least three character types (s.8.2.7).

items.label: Maximum password life
items.detail: For internal users, within the bank's policy (s.8.2.8).

items.label: Shared folder review
items.detail: Permissions on shared resources reviewed at least every six months (s.5.12.1.15).

items.label: Revoke on move or exit
items.detail: Access no longer needed after a transfer or termination is revoked or disabled (s.8.2.4).

cards.back: Identity, qualifications, past employment, civil or criminal proceedings, conflicting outside business and a credit check (framework 3.1.8.4).
Pending proceedings, outside business interests and credit are checked again over time (3.1.8.5).
The framework expects continuous monitoring of employee behaviour to catch insider threats.
Customised programmes for system, database and network administrators and developers (framework 1.3).
Recognised certifications such as CISA, CISSP or CISM for the information security team (2.12(c)).
Training to understand their own roles, alongside physical security and information security staff (2.12(d)).

cards.question: Under the framework, which group must receive training or awareness so they understand their security roles, alongside the bank's own staff?
options: Only the bank's shareholders
Third parties such as vendors and suppliers
Only Bangladesh Bank inspectors
No one outside the bank
cards.explanation: Section 2.12(e) of the framework calls for awareness or training for third parties and vendors so they understand their roles and responsibilities. The guideline also requires a board-approved outsourcing policy and written agreements.

cards.title: Vendors, outsourcing and continuity
cards.body:
Shimul Commercial Bank outsources card personalisation and part of its ATM monitoring. Chapter 12 of the ICT Security Guideline sets the ground rules:

- A **board-approved outsourcing policy** and **written agreements** that set out each party's roles and obligations.
- **Risk-based evaluation** of the provider, and no weakening of the bank's own internal controls.
- The provider must have **disaster recovery** arrangements, and the bank needs **contingency plans** for critical outsourced services.

The framework adds that vendors should get **security awareness** for their roles. For continuity, chapter 9 of the guideline requires a business continuity plan with a disaster recovery plan and site, tested against defined scenarios, including cyber scenarios, with results and lessons recorded.

At Shimul, Anisur's team now samples vendor access logs every quarter, and Proshanta has added a short vendor induction on the bank's security rules.

cards.title: Governance habits that pass an audit
cards.body:
- Keep an **owner** for every system and data set, and make that owner sign off access.
- Put **risk acceptance** in writing, from someone the escalation matrix allows to accept it.
- **Track audit findings** to closure; the guideline expects issues to be followed up and fixed.
- Review **privileged users** on a schedule, not only after an incident.
- Record **training by role**: administrators, developers, executives and vendors each have different needs.

cards.title: Stage 3 take-aways
items: The board approves the ICT strategy and the ICT Security Policy; Steering, Security and Risk Management committees each have defined duties.
The framework requires a qualified, resourced CISO, and four levels of decision from the board to operations.
ICT risk runs through identify, assess, treat, monitor and report, with an ICT risk assessment at least once a year.
Least privilege, prompt revocation, strong passwords, MFA and tight control of privileged and vendor access are core controls.
Internal and external IS audits are at least annual; staff are screened on hiring and periodically, and trained for their roles.

cards.prompt: Pick one system you use at work. Who owns it, who can approve your access, and when was your access last reviewed? If you do not know, who would you ask?

quiz.question: Which body does section 2.1.2 of the ICT Security Guideline say should include representatives from ICT, risk, HR, the cyber security unit, internal control and audit, legal and business units?
options: The board audit committee
The Computer Incident Response Team
The shareholders' general meeting
The ICT Steering Committee
quiz.explanation: The ICT Steering Committee is formed with representatives from ICT, risk, HR, the cyber security unit, ICC and audit, legal and related business units.

quiz.question: How often must a bank carry out an ICT risk assessment under chapter 3 of the guideline?
options: At least once a year
At least once every three years
Only before a new system goes live
Only when Bangladesh Bank asks for one
quiz.explanation: Section 3.2(c) requires an ICT risk assessment at least once a year so risks are identified, assessed and managed.

quiz.question: An officer moves from the foreign trade desk to a retail branch. When should his trade finance system access be removed?
options: At the next quarterly access review
Immediately, as access no longer needed must be revoked
After six months, in case he is transferred back to the trade desk
Only when his new manager asks for it
quiz.explanation: Section 8.2.4 requires access rights that are no longer needed, for example after a transfer or termination, to be revoked or disabled immediately.

quiz.question: A system does not use multi-factor authentication. What minimum password length does the guideline set for it?
options: At least six characters, with at least one number and one capital letter
At least eight characters, with any characters allowed
At least eleven characters, with at least three types of character
At least sixteen characters, letters only
quiz.explanation: Section 8.2.7 sets a minimum of eleven characters where MFA is not used, combining at least three of upper case, lower case, special characters and numbers.

quiz.question: A vendor engineer asks for standing administrator access to the core banking database to speed up support. What does section 8.3.2 of the guideline require?
options: Grant it, provided the vendor contract contains a strong confidentiality clause
No privileged access for vendors without close supervision and monitoring
Grant it, but change the password once a year
Grant it only outside business hours
quiz.explanation: Among the privileged-user controls, the guideline disallows vendors from gaining privileged access to systems without close supervision and monitoring, and bans shared privileged accounts.

quiz.question: Who approves the bank's ICT risk tolerance under section 3.1.3.2 of the guideline?
options: The board or the risk management committee, then communicated to all stakeholders
Each branch manager for their own branch
The external IS auditor during the annual audit
The vendor that hosts the core banking system
quiz.explanation: The bank defines risk tolerance, has it approved by the board or the risk management committee and communicates it to all stakeholders.

quiz.question: Which requirement about the CISO appears in section 2.3.1 of the Cybersecurity Framework?
options: The CISO must report directly to the Head of ICT Division, who signs off the security budget
The CISO role may be combined with the CITO in smaller banks
The CISO must be approved in advance by BFIU
The bank must recruit a qualified CISO and approve the people and budget the role needs
quiz.explanation: Section 2.3.1 asks the organisation to recruit a qualified CISO, approve human resources and a sufficient budget, and expects industry-accepted academic and professional certification.

quiz.question: How often must internal information system audits be done under section 2.4.5 of the guideline?
options: Every two years, alternating with the external audit
Only after a reported security incident
At least once a year, using a risk-based approach
Every quarter for every branch without exception
quiz.explanation: Internal IS audits must be done periodically, at least once a year, following a risk-based approach; reports are kept for the regulator.

quiz.question: During hiring for the data centre team, HR asks what the framework's initial screening should cover. Which list fits section 3.1.8.4?
options: Identity, qualifications, past jobs, civil or criminal proceedings, outside business conflicts and credit
Only identity and a medical fitness certificate
Only academic results and a written test score
Only references from two current colleagues
quiz.explanation: The framework lists identity verification, confirmation of qualifications and previous employment, past or pending proceedings, conflicting external business and a financial credit check.

quiz.question: Section 1.3 of the framework calls for customised training programmes for specific job roles. Which roles does it name?
options: Tellers, cash officers, relationship managers and call centre agents
System, database and network administrators, and developers
Board members and shareholders only
Customers who use internet banking
quiz.explanation: The framework expects regular training for all users and customised programmes for system administrators, database administrators, network administrators and developers.

sessions.title: Cyber Incidents: Response, the 72-Hour Report and Recovery
sessions.summary: Handle a cyber incident the way Bangladesh Bank expects: the incident response plan and CIRT, the framework's incident roles, reporting critical incidents to internal and external stakeholders, including BGD-CIRT and Bangladesh Bank, within 72 hours, the national CERT duty under the Cyber Security Act 2026, the PDPA breach notice, backups, recovery and lessons learned, with extra care for SWIFT.
objectives: Describe the incident response plan, the CIRT and the framework's incident roles from the MD to unit supervisors
Apply the 72-hour reporting rule for critical cyber incidents and know the other notification routes
Follow the guideline's SWIFT controls and the framework's backup, testing and recovery expectations
Run a post-incident review and turn lessons into training

cards.title: Friday night alert
cards.setting: Security Operations Centre, Shimul Commercial Bank data centre, Mirpur. 11:48 pm, Thursday, two weeks later.

lines.text: The SOC has flagged ransomware activity on three servers in the remittance processing network. Files are being encrypted. A ransom note just appeared.
I'm the incident response team leader. Isolate those servers from the network now. Who else is on the call?
Audit is here as an observer. We need a clean timeline: when did it start, and when did we know?
Customers in Khulna are already texting that inward remittances haven't arrived.
Then the clock is running. Let's work through this properly.

scenes.heading: Preparation
scenes.narration: A written incident response plan, reviewed every year, sets roles, contacts, procedures, backup and recovery steps and the legal reporting duties. People are trained for their roles with simulated events.

scenes.heading: Detection and analysis
scenes.narration: Monitoring tools, the security operations centre and staff reports raise alerts. Trained people available round the clock decide whether an event is a real incident and how severe it is.

scenes.heading: Containment, eradication and recovery
scenes.narration: Isolate affected systems, remove the threat and restore services from clean backups, without destroying the evidence forensic investigators need.

scenes.heading: Post-incident activity
scenes.narration: Report as required, review what happened and why, and feed the lessons into procedures, training and tests.

cards.title: Who does what in a cyber incident (framework 2.5)
cards.caption: The framework suggests a pocket card with the team's emergency contacts for every employee.

items.label: Incident Management Leader
items.detail: MD or delegate: manages high-severity incidents and decides on business changes; deals with the media.

items.label: Incident Management Coordinator
items.detail: Head of ICT or CITO: coordinates divisions and leads recovery.

items.label: Response Team Leader
items.detail: Head of information security or CISO: single contact for users; evaluates and escalates.

items.label: Response Team members
items.detail: Division and unit supervisors: act after a briefing from the team leader.

cards.question: Under the framework's incident roles, who may speak to the media about a cyber incident?
options: Any branch manager whose customers are affected
The Cyber Incident Management Leader (the MD or delegate) or a person they designate
The ICT vendor's account manager
The first officer who noticed the incident
cards.explanation: Section 2.5 says only the Incident Management Leader, normally the MD, or a person designated by them deals with the media.

cards.title: The 72-hour rule and other routes
cards.body:
Section 8.1.2.1 of the Cybersecurity Framework: for any **critical cyber incident**, the bank must report to **internal stakeholders** (relevant business units, senior management, the board) and **external stakeholders** (customers, critical service providers, **BGD-CIRT** and **Bangladesh Bank**) **within 72 hours from the time of occurrence**.

The clock starts when the incident **occurred**, not when it was found, so late detection eats into the window.

Other routes to know:

- The **ICT Security Guideline**: the bank's CIRT cooperates with and reports to **Bangladesh Bank's CIRT**.
- The **Cyber Security Act 2026** says any public or private organisation that suffers a cyber incident must inform the **national CERT** under the National Cyber Security Agency **without delay**.
- The **Personal Data Protection Act 2026**: notify the **Authority** of a personal data breach likely to cause significant harm, as regulations set.

Your incident procedure should map each route and owner.

cards.title: Match the duty to its source
cards.prompt: Link each reporting or response duty to the document that sets it.

pairs.left: Critical incident to BGD-CIRT and Bangladesh Bank within 72 hours
CIRT cooperates and reports to Bangladesh Bank CIRT
Inform the national CERT without delay after a cyber incident
Notify the Authority of a breach likely to cause significant harm
Incident response plan reviewed every year

items.label: Encryption begins
items.detail: Later forensic work shows the attack started here: the 72-hour clock runs from occurrence.

items.label: SOC alert
items.detail: Analysts confirm ransomware on three servers.

items.label: Containment
items.detail: Servers isolated; incident team leader escalates to the coordinator and the MD.

items.label: Classified critical
items.detail: Remittance service down; internal reporting to senior management and the board begins.

items.label: 72-hour limit
items.detail: Reports to BGD-CIRT, Bangladesh Bank and other stakeholders must be in by now.

cards.title: The ransom question
cards.setting: Crisis room, head office. 10:15 am, Friday.

lines.text: Backups of the remittance database ran last night at 8 pm, before the attack started. We tested restoring them in September.
And the attackers want payment in crypto within 48 hours, or they threaten to publish customer data.
If customer data leaks, my branch will be flooded with frightened people.
The framework is blunt on ransom. And if personal data was taken, we have a data protection angle too.

cards.title: Pay, restore or wait?
cards.situation: Shimul has clean, tested backups of the affected remittance database from before the attack. The attackers demand payment and threaten to leak customer data. Forensics has not yet confirmed whether data left the network. The incident occurred about 13 hours ago.

choices.text: Restore from clean backups after removing the threat, keep evidence, assess whether personal data was taken, and send the required reports within 72 hours of occurrence.
choices.outcome: Best. The framework says paying a ransom does not guarantee data comes back, expects tested backups and recovery, and requires critical incidents to be reported within 72 hours. A data breach assessment decides the PDPA notice.

choices.text: Pay quickly to stop the leak, then restore systems quietly without reporting, since data may not have left.
choices.outcome: Poor. Paying gives no guarantee, may fund crime and does not remove the reporting duty for a critical incident.

choices.text: Restore from backups but wait until forensics is completely finished before telling anyone outside the bank.
choices.outcome: Partly right on recovery, but forensics can take weeks. The 72-hour window runs from occurrence, so reporting cannot wait for a perfect picture.

choices.text: Wipe and rebuild all servers at once to get services back fastest.
choices.outcome: Risky. It may restore service, but it destroys forensic evidence the bank and investigators need and may miss how attackers got in.

items.label: Automated backups
items.detail: Or more often, depending on how sensitive and critical the data is.

items.label: Backup restore tests
items.detail: Test recovery for a sample of in-scope assets at least every quarter.

items.label: Incident exercises
items.detail: Incident response exercises for key people at least once a year.

items.label: Critical incident report
items.detail: From the time of occurrence (framework 8.1.2.1).

cards.title: Handle a suspected critical incident
cards.prompt: Put Shimul's steps in the right order.
steps: Detect and confirm the incident; record the time it is believed to have started
Contain: isolate affected systems while preserving evidence
Escalate through the incident team leader to the coordinator and the MD
Report the critical incident internally and to BGD-CIRT, Bangladesh Bank and other stakeholders within 72 hours
Eradicate the threat and recover from clean, tested backups
Hold a post-incident review and update procedures and training

cards.title: Payments under attack: the SWIFT controls
Lessons the framework asks banks to learn

cards.back: No. The framework warns banks never to rely on MFA alone for critical assets, because attackers can sometimes defeat it.

cards.front: Will paying the ransom get data back?
cards.back: There is no guarantee. The framework tells banks to understand this, and to rely on backups instead.

cards.front: Can known risks wait because another layer exists?
cards.back: No. Leaving several known risks open because 'another control will catch it' is exactly what the framework warns against.

cards.front: What is the first aim of lessons learned?
cards.back: To educate employees and customers on protecting the confidentiality, integrity and availability of the bank's information.

cards.front: When must a cybersecurity audit happen?
cards.back: At least once a year, and after any security breach or cyber attack.

cards.question: Shimul's incident started at 9:30 pm on Thursday but was confirmed at 11:48 pm. From when does the framework's 72-hour reporting window run?
options: From 11:48 pm, when the SOC confirmed it
From 9:30 pm on Thursday, the time of occurrence
From Monday morning, the first full working day
From when the board is told
cards.explanation: Section 8.1.2.1 says the report to internal and external stakeholders is due within 72 hours from the time of occurrence, so slow detection shortens the time left.

cards.title: Your part in an incident
cards.body:
- **Report fast** through the bank's channel, even if you are not sure it is serious.
- **Do not switch off or wipe** a suspect PC unless told to; unplug it from the network if instructed.
- **Write down times** and what you saw; the 72-hour clock runs from occurrence.
- **Do not talk to the media or post online**; only the MD or a designated person speaks for the bank.
- **Join the drills.** The guideline wants simulated events in incident training for a reason.

cards.title: Stage 4 take-aways
items: Every bank needs an incident response plan reviewed annually, a trained CIRT and people able to respond 24/7.
Framework roles: the MD leads high-severity incidents and media, the CITO coordinates, the CISO leads the response team.
Critical cyber incidents go to internal and external stakeholders, including BGD-CIRT and Bangladesh Bank, within 72 hours of occurrence.
The Cyber Security Act 2026 adds a duty to inform the national CERT without delay; the PDPA adds a breach notice to the Authority.
Weekly backups, quarterly restore tests, annual exercises, strict SWIFT controls and honest post-incident reviews keep the bank resilient.

cards.prompt: If your PC showed a ransom note right now, who would you call first, and do you have the number? Note the gaps you find and raise them with your manager.

quiz.question: Under the Cybersecurity Framework, within what time must a critical cyber incident be reported to internal and external stakeholders, including Bangladesh Bank?
options: Within 24 hours from the time of discovery
Within 7 days from the end of the investigation
By the end of the following month
Within 72 hours from the time of occurrence
quiz.explanation: Section 8.1.2.1 requires reporting of any critical cyber incident within 72 hours from the time of occurrence to stakeholders such as BGD-CIRT and Bangladesh Bank.

quiz.question: Which external stakeholders does section 8.1.2.1 of the framework list for critical incident reports?
options: Only the bank's external auditor
Shareholders, the stock exchanges and the securities regulator only
Customers, critical service providers, BGD-CIRT and Bangladesh Bank
Only the police and the courts
quiz.explanation: The framework lists customers, critical service providers, BGD-CIRT and Bangladesh Bank as external stakeholders, alongside internal reporting to business units, senior management and the board.

quiz.question: Who does the framework name as the Cyber Incident Response Team Leader and single point of contact for users?
options: The Managing Director or the delegated deputy
The head of information security or CISO
The head of human resources
The external forensic investigator
quiz.explanation: Section 2.5 makes the head of information security or CISO the team leader and one-point contact; the MD is the Incident Management Leader and the CITO the coordinator.

quiz.question: How often must the incident response plan be reviewed and updated under section 6.3.2 of the ICT Security Guideline?
options: Every five years, with the ICT strategy
Only when Bangladesh Bank issues a new version of the guideline
Only after a critical incident has occurred
Every year, to reflect system changes and problems found
quiz.explanation: Section 6.3.2 asks the bank to review and update the incident response plan annually, taking account of system changes and issues found in use or testing.

quiz.question: A ransomware gang offers to return encrypted files if the bank pays. What does the framework tell banks to understand?
options: Paying is acceptable if the board approves it within 24 hours
Paying removes the need to report the incident
Paying a ransom does not guarantee the data will be returned
Paying is required when backups are older than a week
quiz.explanation: Among its lessons learned, the framework says paying a ransom does not guarantee that encrypted data will be returned, and stresses the importance of backups.

quiz.question: How often does the framework expect banks to test recovery from backups for a sample of in-scope assets?
options: At least quarterly
At least once every two years
Only when a disaster happens
Only during the annual external audit
quiz.explanation: Section 7.1.1.12 asks for backup recovery testing quarterly or more often; section 7.1.1.10 asks for automated backups at least weekly.

quiz.question: Under the Cyber Security Act 2026, what must an organisation do when it suffers a cyber incident?
options: Inform the National Data Management Authority within 30 days
Inform only its own board at the next meeting
Inform the national CERT, but only if a declared critical information infrastructure is affected
Inform the national CERT under the National Cyber Security Agency without delay
quiz.explanation: Section 9 of the Act provides that any public, private or autonomous organisation where a cyber incident occurs must inform the national CERT under the Agency without delay.

quiz.question: Which of these is one of the SWIFT controls in section 11.8 of the ICT Security Guideline?
options: Multi-factor authentication for user sign-on is mandatory
Super-user profiles are allowed for faster processing
Internet access on SWIFT client PCs should stay open for updates
Passwords may be kept in a text file on the server
quiz.explanation: Section 11.8 makes MFA for sign-on mandatory, bans super key profiles, restricts internet and USB access and forbids storing passwords on servers.

quiz.question: An officer's PC shows a ransom note. What should she do first?
options: Restart the PC to see whether the note disappears
Post a warning on social media for customers
Report it at once through the incident channel and follow instructions, without wiping the PC
Copy her files to a USB drive before anything else
quiz.explanation: Prompt reporting starts the response; restarting, wiping or copying can spread malware or destroy evidence, and only designated people speak publicly.

quiz.question: How often does the framework require a cybersecurity audit?
options: Every three years, or whenever a new CISO joins the bank's management
At least once a year, and after any breach or cyber attack
Only when the external auditor requests one
Monthly, by the branch manager for each branch
quiz.explanation: Section 8.1.3 calls for a cybersecurity audit at least once a year and after any incident or attack, by internal teams or external companies.

sessions.title: Personal Data, the Cyber Security Act and Readiness for 31 December 2026
sessions.summary: Pull it together: the Personal Data Protection Act 2026 and the Code of Conduct on customer data, the Cyber Security Act 2026 on critical information infrastructure and offences, and the programme Bangladesh Bank expects to see by 31 December 2026: training by audience, records and KPIs, audits, compliance plans and dispensation.
objectives: Explain the PDPA 2026 basics: consent, purpose limits, security, retention, breach notice and data subjects' rights
Describe what the Cyber Security Act 2026 means for a bank: the Agency, critical information infrastructure and offences
Build a training plan that meets the guideline and framework for every audience, with records and KPIs
Prepare evidence for an inspection: policies, audits, risk assessments, incident records and compliance plans

cards.title: Six weeks to the deadline
cards.setting: CISO's office, head office. 9:00 am, 18 November 2026.

lines.text: Six weeks until 31 December. The board wants a readiness report, and Bangladesh Bank's ICT inspectors may visit early next year.
I've pulled the training records. Annual awareness is at 82 percent. The 60-day email session is the weak spot for staff who joined branches mid-year.
Customers keep asking whether we're allowed to share their data with our insurance partner. My staff aren't sure what the new data law says.
And I need evidence, not promises: policies, minutes, test results, incident reports, training logs.
Final stage: the Compliance Summit. Let's climb it.

cards.title: The Personal Data Protection Act 2026 in five moves

scenes.heading: Data belongs to the person
scenes.narration: The Act treats a person's personal data as theirs. The bank, as a data fiduciary, processes it on their behalf and must be able to show it acts lawfully.

scenes.heading: Consent, or another lawful basis
scenes.narration: Consent must be freely given, specific, clear and possible to withdraw, after telling the person the purpose, how long data is kept, any transfer and how to withdraw. Some other bases, such as performing a contract with the person, also apply.

scenes.heading: Use it only for its purpose
scenes.narration: Personal data may not be disclosed for a purpose other than the one it was collected for without the person's consent, subject to the Act's other provisions.

scenes.heading: Secure it and keep it only as long as needed
scenes.narration: Banks must use suitable technical and organisational measures, such as pseudonymisation and encryption, and must not keep data beyond the period regulations allow.

scenes.heading: Breaches and the Authority
scenes.narration: A breach likely to cause significant harm must be notified to the National Data Management Authority in the form and time regulations set.

cards.title: Customer data: two layers of duty
cards.caption: Both apply at once. The Act's complaint, fine and compensation sections and the Chief Data Officer duty start on a later date the Government will notify.

items.label: Core rule
items.left: Keep customers' affairs and account details secret
items.right: No disclosure beyond the collection purpose without consent

items.label: Security
items.right: Technical and organisational measures, e.g. encryption

items.label: If it goes wrong
items.right: Notify the Authority of serious breaches; complaints and fines later

cards.question: Sumaiya's customer opened a savings account. The bank's insurance partner wants the customer's phone number for marketing. What does the PDPA 2026 require?
options: Share it, because the customer already gave it to the bank
Do not disclose it for this new purpose without the customer's consent
Share it if the partner signs a confidentiality letter
Share it only with customers who have loans
cards.explanation: Section 16 bars disclosing personal data for any purpose other than the one it was collected for without consent. The Code of Conduct also requires secrecy of customers' affairs.

cards.title: The PDPA's moving parts for a bank
cards.body:
Key points from the **Personal Data Protection Act 2026** (Act 63 of 2026):

- **In force:** deemed effective from **6 November 2025**, except section 23 (Chief Data Officer) and sections 31-35 (complaints, administrative fines, compensation). Those start on a date the Government notifies after 18 months.
- **Consent (section 5):** freely given, specific, clear and withdrawable; the person must be told the purpose, retention period, transfers and how to withdraw. The **burden of proving consent is on the bank**.
- **Other lawful bases:** for example performing a contract with the person.
- **Rights:** access and portability, correction and updating, and withdrawal of consent, on written request.
- **Security (section 17):** proportionate measures, including pseudonymisation, encryption, resilience and regular testing.
- **Retention (section 18):** no longer than regulations allow for the purpose.
- **Breach (section 20):** notify the Authority of a breach likely to cause significant harm.
- **Chief Data Officer (section 23):** significant data fiduciaries will need one.

cards.title: Which law or rule?
cards.prompt: Sort each duty to its main source.

items.text: Prove that a customer's consent was validly given
Notify the Authority of a personal data breach likely to cause significant harm
Appoint a Chief Data Officer once that section comes into force
Government may declare a system critical information infrastructure
Unauthorised e-transactions from a bank are a criminal offence
Email security session for new joiners within 60 days
Critical cyber incidents reported to Bangladesh Bank within 72 hours
Annual security awareness training for all staff

cards.title: The Cyber Security Act 2026 for bankers

cards.back: Act 81 of 2026, passed on 10 April 2026 and deemed in force from 21 May 2025. It replaced the Cyber Security Ordinance 2025 and was amended again in July 2026.
A National Cyber Security Agency, headed by a Director General and attached to the ICT Division, with a national CERT and a national security operations centre.
The Government may declare systems or networks as critical; the list is updated at least once a year (section 15).

cards.front: What if the bank's system is declared critical?
cards.back: It faces monitoring and inspection by the Director General and must audit its infrastructure every year and report to the National Cyber Security Council (section 16).
Illegal access, damage to systems, cyber forgery and fraud, and e-transactions from a bank or MFS provider without lawful authority (section 24).
Up to one year's imprisonment and a fine of up to Tk 10 lakh under section 24, as the Act currently reads.

lines.text: Our biggest gap: 140 staff who joined branches between July and September have passed 60 days without the email security session. The classroom slots in Dhaka were full.
Branch staff can't easily travel to Dhaka. Could it be online?
The guideline lets the bank choose delivery methods, including e-learning. What it cares about is that it happens on time and we can prove it.
Then we need a fix for these 140 and a plan so it never slips again.

cards.title: Closing the 60-day gap
cards.situation: 140 recent joiners have passed 60 days without the email security session required by section 5.14.9 of the ICT Security Guideline. The board readiness report is due in two weeks.

choices.text: Run the session for all 140 now through e-learning or virtual classes, record completion, report the gap and fix honestly, and build the session into every induction from day one.
choices.outcome: Best. The guideline lets banks choose methods such as e-learning. Fixing the gap, recording it and changing the process is what inspectors look for.

choices.text: Mark the 140 as complete because they attended general induction, which mentioned email briefly.
choices.outcome: Poor. Recording training that did not cover phishing detection, etiquette and incident reporting is a false record and will not survive an audit.

choices.text: Wait until January and include them in the annual awareness campaign.
choices.outcome: Partly helpful, as they would eventually be trained, but the 60-day breach continues and the board report would hide a known gap.

choices.text: Ask Bangladesh Bank for dispensation from the 60-day rule.
choices.outcome: Not suitable here. Dispensation is for exceptional, persistent non-compliance; this gap can be closed within days.

cards.title: Training plan by audience
cards.caption: Add vendors' security awareness and the bank's customer education campaigns to complete the picture.

items.label: All staff
items.detail: Awareness on joining and every year; periodic cyber hygiene training.

items.label: New joiners
items.detail: Email security session within 60 days; foundation training for new officers.

items.label: Managers and executives
items.detail: ICT infrastructure, policies, governance and incident duties.

items.label: Privileged users and ICT staff
items.detail: Role programmes for admins and developers; professional certifications.

items.label: CIRT and SOC
items.detail: Incident training with simulations; national and international drills.

cards.title: Get ready for the inspection
